text.p: German authorities on Thursday said they had seized sausages suspected of containing illegally imported British beef.

A worldwide ban on exports of British beef was imposed in March 1996 because of fears some might be infected by bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), or mad cow disease which could trigger an equivalent deadly ailment in humans, Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease.
The North Rhine-Westphalia state environment ministry in Germany said it had confiscated around 33 tonnes of beef that had been purchased by three German firms from the Belgian company Tragex-Gel.
One of the German firms made sausages out of the beef but the ministry said none of the meat had made it onto the market. The beef was now being examined by officials.
Belgium earlier this month blocked all meat -- whatever its stated origin -- either handled or bearing the name of Belgian firms NV Tragex-Gel and SA Lefebre.
The two firms have appealed against the ban. Neither company was available for comment on Thursday night on the German state environment ministry's allegations.

The German move came after the European Commission said it had traced 1,6000 tonnes of British beef illegally imported to the Netherlands, Egypt and Russia either via Belgium or using Belgian certificates.
"The ... energy with which the Belgian firms have acted has deeply shocked me," North Rhine-Westphalia environment minister Baerbel Hoehn said in a statement.

"If it is discovered that the Belgian firms even imported meat possibly infected with BSE, then the controls in Britain as well those of the British authorities and the (European) Commission have completely failed," Hoehn said.

German prosecutors on Wednesday confirmed that a separate 172 tonnes of frozen beef seized two weeks ago in the north of the country was British meat imported via France with Belgian papers and intended for export to Russia.
Germany, where millions of sausages are consumed every year, led the fight for a European Union ban on British beef.
